claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is identified as the same alloy system as five-component CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial alloy structure is FCC.
The initial dislocation density is near zero.
Dislocations in the HEA nucleate homogeneously at free surfaces because of surface stress concentration.
Dislocation nucleation does not initiate at vacancy clusters.
The nucleated defects are Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vector 1/6<112>.
Shockley partial dislocations glide on {111} planes and create intrinsic stacking faults.
The <110> loading orientation has a higher maximum yield strength than the <11-1> orientation.
The orientation dependence of maximum yield strength is caused by differences in resolved shear stress on {111} slip planes.
The HCP-like regions are a percolating network of intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
A percolating stacking-fault network can unlock Lomer-Cottrell locks.
Lomer-Cottrell locks form through interactions among moving partial dislocations and contribute to work hardening.
Increasing temperature lowers the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation and thereby increases dislocation density.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases from 77 K to 1000 K.
Dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases with increasing temperature.
The apparent HCP fraction increases with strain and temperature.
CNA or center-of-symmetry analysis combined with bond-angle distributions can discriminate stacking faults from a true HCP transformation.
Stacking faults should exhibit a continuous gradient of local order without a distinct HCP lattice-parameter shift.
A true HCP transformation should produce a discrete lattice-parameter change, a sharp phase boundary, and a distinct HCP-related RDF peak.
The proposed behavior applies over strain rates of 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1 and temperatures of 77 to 1000 K.

contradictions.description: The material is alternately called equiatomic FeNiCrMn, a four-element alloy, and CoCrFeMnNi/CoNiCrFeMn, a five-element alloy containing Co. These are not compositionally equivalent labels.

The mechanism states that increasing temperature increases dislocation density by lowering the nucleation barrier, whereas the predicted outcome states that dislocation density decreases with temperature and is highest at 77 K.

The stated scope includes nanocrystalline alloys but then excludes polycrystalline samples with significant grain-boundary effects; nanocrystalline materials are ordinarily polycrystalline and strongly influenced by grain boundaries.
